title: Minimum Number of Operations to Make All Array Elements Equal to 1
statement:
You get an array `nums` of positive integers, of length `n`. In one operation you pick two neighbouring positions `i` and `i + 1` (with `0 <= i < n - 1`) and overwrite one of `nums[i]` and `nums[i + 1]` (your choice) with the greatest common divisor of the two values. You may do this as often as you like.

Return the smallest number of operations after which every element of `nums` is `1`, or `-1` if that can never happen.
notes:
## Intuition

Once some element equals `1`, every neighbour can be turned into `1` with one operation (the gcd of `1` and anything is `1`), and that `1` spreads outward. So with `ones` ones already present, each other element needs exactly one operation: the answer is `n - ones`.

With no `1` at all, we must first create one. An operation can only ever produce the gcd of a contiguous stretch of the array, so a `1` can appear only if some stretch `nums[left..right]` has gcd `1`. Folding such a stretch from one end takes `right - left` operations, so we want the shortest such stretch. After that, the `n - 1` other elements each take one more operation. If even the whole array has gcd greater than `1`, no `1` can ever appear.

## Approach

1. Count `ones`. If there is at least one, return `n - ones`.
2. For every start `left`, extend `right` one step at a time, keeping `current = gcd(nums[left..right])`.
3. The first time `current` becomes `1`, record `right - left` in `shortest` and stop extending (a longer stretch only costs more).
4. If `shortest` was never set, return `-1`; otherwise return `shortest + n - 1`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 6, 3, 4]`, `n = 4`, no ones.

- `left = 0`: gcd(2, 6) = 2, gcd(2, 3) = 1 at `right = 2`, so `shortest = 2`.
- `left = 1`: gcd(6, 3) = 3, gcd(3, 4) = 1 at `right = 3`; 2 is not better.
- `left = 2`: gcd(3, 4) = 1 at `right = 3`, so `shortest = 1`.

The answer is `1 + 4 - 1 = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · log M): every pair `(left, right)` costs one gcd on values up to M = 10^6.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- When some elements are already `1`, nothing needs creating and those elements cost nothing: the answer is `n - ones`.
- Creating the first `1` from a stretch of length k costs `k - 1` operations, not k.
- When no stretch has gcd `1`, return `-1`; checking only adjacent pairs misses longer stretches like `[6, 10, 15]`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `gcd` | Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor |
| `ones` | how many elements already equal `1` |
| `left`, `right` | ends of the stretch being examined |
| `current` | gcd of `nums[left..right]` |
| `shortest` | fewest operations found to create the first `1` |
